5162.prule: No rule is stated in any reachable source; the record rests on transcription data, not on an author's statement. Two independent 1971 SIL-format field transcriptions (Hall, Kayawan/Manay; the Caraga list in Zorc's folder) mark stress with a tick before the stressed syllable. Most marked words are penultimate ('bana, 'katol, 'kilat, 'pasak, 'gabi, 'ilong, 'otaw, 'gosok, ma'pasoq, ti'naqi, ko'midya, mati'kadong, kalin'toqo); a clear minority are final (ba'lyay, mara'ig, ka'mon, wa'lya, ma'niq, ta'nom, bira'qon, bo'lyaq; Caraga maka'gat, o'sog, ka'mon), with near-minimal contrasts (Hall 228 bo'lyaq vs 229 'polyaq; Hall 176 'osog vs Caraga 176 o'sog on the same item) and no weight or segmental conditioning visible (penults are open CV under both patterns; closed finals occur under both: 'pasak, 'kilat vs ka'mon, ta'nom). Some trisyllables carry the tick on the initial syllable ('sipaqon, 'kilaya, 'kawalya, 'sanggatos, 'patayan, 'kilalya, 'tampong). (Bisayan/Mansakan) type.

5162.cfw: No published phonology of Mandaya states a stress rule, but two 1971 SIL survey wordlists that mark stress syllable by syllable, Hall (1971) for Kayawan (Manay) and an unsigned Caraga list preserved in Zorc's Mansakan field folder, agree that most words are stressed on the penult while a lexical minority (ba'lyay 'house', ta'nom 'plant', mata'mis 'sweet', ko'sog, ka'mon) are stressed on the final syllable, the ordinary Central Philippine contrast, and nothing else written on the language (Gallman 1979, Pasion & Sandoval 2013, Galvez 2018, Duping 2021) contradicts this.

5163.prule: No stress placement rule is stated by either reachable description. Meinhof 1916-17: 217 reports that when first writing Katla he believed a dynamic (stress) accent was present and marked a number of notes with ′ (Stärkeakzent), then convinced himself that musical tones exist alongside the dynamic accent, as in other Sudanic languages; on p. 218 he adds that he had often, especially at first, taken the high tone for a stress accent, that his two informants (B. = Bechid, S. = Somnu Kordofani, p. 212) often agree in tone, and that the tone laws are left to future research; the position of the dynamic accent is never stated and no stressed syllable is identified. Tucker & Bryan 1966: 263 (after Stevenson) likewise: 'Stevenson notes the existence of both tone and stress, and gives examples of a few lexical tone doublets'; examples are not otherwise tone-marked; stress is never marked or located.
5163.srule: Not mentioned in Meinhof 1916-17, 'Zur Tonlehre', pp. 217-219 (whole section): a dynamic (stress) accent is said to exist beside the musical tones, but no stressed syllable, primary or secondary, is ever located; Tucker & Bryan 1966: 263 (after Stevenson) likewise only 'both tone and stress'.

5163.tone: Meinhof 1916-17: 217-219: Katla has 'musikalische Töne' 'neben dem dynamischen Akzent'; he first believed a dynamic (stress) accent was present, later concluded that musical tones exist alongside it, and admits 'Den Hochton habe ich, wie es leicht geschieht, besonders zuerst oft, als Stärkeakzent aufgefaßt' (p. 218), i.e. many of his stress percepts were the high tone. Katla data on p. 218 are marked with high and low tones (Hochton, Tiefton), with the same word often noted with different tones by the two informants B. and S.; tones appear 'sogar auf stimmhaften Konsonanten'; Klingenheben ('Klg.') also noted pitch and recorded tone changes in context (gu 'Hund' changes tone between high tones; mumwin 'Elefant' after a high tone). The remarks on Mittelton and sentence tone change ('in vielen Tonsprachen... Tiefton zwischen Hochtönen wird Mittelton, Hochtöne am Schluß werden tief') are general, not Katla-specific. Tones are marked only in the wordlist and sentences; 'Nähere Untersuchung über ihre Gesetze muß der Einzelforschung überlassen bleiben.' Nothing on stress placement, pitch accent, or tone-stress interaction beyond the perceptual confusion. tn.quote: Bei dem Versuch, das Katla zu schreiben, glaubte ich erst, daß ein dynamischer Akzent vorläge. Eine Reihe von Notizen sind deshalb mit ′ d. h. mit Stärkeakzent versehen. Später überzeugte ich mich, daß neben dem dynamischen Akzent musikalische Töne vorliegen wie in andern Sudansprachen. ... Den Hochton habe ich, wie es leicht geschieht, besonders zuerst oft, als Stärkeakzent aufgefaßt. ... Es kam nur darauf an, das Vorhandensein der musikalischen Töne nachzuweisen, und das ist, so viel ich sehe, gelungen. Nähere Untersuchung über ihre Gesetze muß der Einzelforschung überlassen bleiben.
tn.translation: When attempting to write Katla I at first believed that a dynamic (stress) accent was present. A number of notes are therefore marked with ′, i.e. with stress accent. Later I convinced myself that alongside the dynamic accent musical tones are present, as in other Sudan languages. ... The high tone I have often, as easily happens, especially at first, taken for stress accent. ... The point was only to demonstrate the presence of the musical tones, and that, as far as I can see, has succeeded. Closer investigation of their laws must be left to specialised research.

tn.note: Meinhof asserts 'musical tones' (high and low marked, a few circumflexes) beside a dynamic accent he never locates and often mistook for high tone; no tone count or rules given.

5164.srule: In words of four or more syllables a minor (secondary) stress falls on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress, i.e. two syllables before the primary (karikara /karikárə/ 'village'; Brown 1986 p.xiv /kàrikára/); compounds show the same pattern (maeamariti /màeamaríti/ 'shame'). Only one minor stress is stated; iteration in words of six or more syllables is not described. Stated for Toaripi (p.307), extended to Orokolo (p.350) and restated for both in Brown 1986 p.xiv; applies to Keoru-Ahia only through Brown's classification of Keuru (Belepa) and Aheave as dialects closely affiliated with Orokolo.

5165.prule: None: no word-stress rule. Kɔnni is a tone language (two basic tone levels, High and Low, plus a downstepped High after a High, sec. 6.1.1 p. 338; tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive). Cahill examines stress explicitly (sec. 6.7) and finds no phonetic correlate (vowel length, amplitude) that is significant and independent of tone: in two words with the same LH tone sequence on the first two syllables, greater amplitude falls on the second syllable in kùléhé 'the tortoises' but on the first in kùlí 'tortoise'. 5165.tone: Two basic tone levels, High and Low, with a downstepped High after a High (sec. 6.1.1, p. 338; minimal and near-minimal tone pairs listed there); downstep treated as the phonetic result of a floating Low; floating High as the associative morpheme; tonal polarity (chapter 6 overview, p. 39). 5167.dq: primary stress is assigned to the main verb if it is not part of the major presupposition of the sentence, and to the head of the focus NP if the main verb is presupposed.
5167.dloc: p. 29, section 3 'Phonological rules', A 'Pre-cycle rules', (a) 'Stress assignment'; tone statement p. 22, section 'Non-consonants'.
5167.prule: Sentence-level, syntax-assigned: primary stress falls on the main verb unless the verb is part of the major presupposition of the sentence, in which case it falls on the head of the focus NP (examples 1-2: the same string 'Asa is here' is stressed on 'here' as an answer to 'Where is Asa?' and on 'is' as an answer to 'What is Asa doing?'). No word-level position rule is stated.
5167.srule: Sentence-level, assigned by the syntax like the primary: secondary stress on the first syllable of the head noun of each component NP and of the head verb when these have not received primary stress; tertiary stress on syntactic markers (for a bisyllabic marker the stressed syllable is specified by the syntactic component). No word-internal rhythmic/alternating stress is described.
5167.quote: The assignment of primary stress is difficult to state without a detailed explanation of the syntactic component of Lisu grammar. Surface strings from that component are assigned linear order by topicalisation and focus rules (see Hope 1972) and primary stress is assigned to the main verb if it is not part of the major presupposition of the sentence, and to the head of the focus NP if the main verb is presupposed. ... 5167.tone: Tone language: p. 22 'All syllabic segments will be specified for tone, and thus, since syllables rather than segments are distinguished by tone, the pitch features are not given as distinctive features of vowels in the following chart' (spacing normalised). 5173.prule: No reached source states a stress rule for Mudu Koraga or for any Koraga variety. The only Mudu-specific description, Bhat 1971 ch. 4 'Mudu Koraga' sec. 1 Phonology (pp. 33-34), read in full, gives only the phonemic inventory (1.1), allophony of n and a (1.2), cluster and distribution restrictions (1.3) and minimal-pair contrasts (1.4); both scan layers grepped for stress|accent|intonation|pitch|prominen|loud yield only 'equal prominence' (p. 23, canonical shapes of Tappu verbal bases). Krishnamurti 2003 p. 27 (sec. 1.5.1) gives only a Dravidian-wide, hedged generalisation that names no Koraga variety: 'There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.' The same book's sec. 2.4.1 (pp. 58-59, Google Books) gives Telugu a weight-sensitive rule ('The stress falls on the first syllable if it is short; it falls on the second syllable which follows a short syllable and if it has a long vowel'), so the p. 27 default is not uniform across the family and cannot be transferred to an undescribed language as a fixed quantity-insensitive rule. 5177.dflt: penult: two light syllables form one right-aligned trochee (['mɑ̞ko] /mɑ.ko/ 'no, not', [ɑ̞nu̞'nu̞zi̞] /ɑ.nu.nu.zi/ 'their souls', ['ɑ̞mɑ̞] /ɑ.mɑ/ 'Daddy', [t̪ i̞ 'lɑ̞lɑ̞] /ti-lɑ.lɑ/ '3PL habitually go' with the prefix skipped); a lone CV word is a degenerate stressed foot (te 'ocean', li 'poison', lu 'armband', mbi 'Trochus', pa, to)
5177.prule: Stress is predictable and quantity-sensitive: bimoraic (moraic) trochees are built from right to left over the word, with long vowels/vowel sequences and a coda consonant after a short vowel making a syllable heavy. Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot, so in the transcribed examples the final syllable is stressed when heavy ([i̞ 'rɑ̞:β] /i-rɑɑβ/ 'go sailing', [i̞ 'sɛŋ] /i-sɛŋ/ 'knock', [nɑ'u̞m] /nɑ.um/ '1SG-steal', [ɑ̞i't̪ ɑ̞r] /ɑi.tɑr/ 'large wooden spoon', [mɑ̞'lɑ̞u̞] /mɑ.lɑu/ 'for a long time', [t̪ ɑ̞mɑ̞'mɑ̞i̞] /tɑmɑmɑi/ '1PL exclusive father', [ɑ̞ŋɑ̞'ŋɑ̞o] /ɑ.ŋɑ.ŋɑo/ 'spider'); a long-vowel syllable is stressed and the consonant or syllable after it is extrametrical ([ɑ̞ri̞ 'ɑ̞:ŋ] /ɑ.ri.ɑɑŋ/, [i̞ pɑ̞du'du:ŋ] /i-pɑduduuŋ/ 'correct, teach', [t̪ i̞ n't̪ i̞:nɑ̞] /tintiinɑ/ 'big ones', ['ɑ̞:t̪ ɛ] /ɑɑtɛ/ 'his liver'); otherwise the penult is stressed (['mɑ̞ko] /mɑ.ko/ 'no, not', [ɑ̞nu̞'nu̞zi̞] /ɑ.nu.nu.zi/ 'their souls', ['ɑ̞mɑ̞] /ɑ.mɑ/ 'Daddy'). Never stressed (extrametrical): a final consonant or syllable after a long vowel, the subject-indexing prefixes ([t̪ i̞ 'lɑ̞] /ti-lɑ/ '3PL-go', [u̞'lɑ̞] /u-lɑ/ '2SG-go'), word-final transitive suffixes, and the plural prefix -xa on inalienable nouns. Monosyllabic CV words form degenerate one-syllable feet and are stressed. Stress is manifested by increased amplitude, length and pitch; vowel length is contrastive independently of stress (p. 8 minimal pairs). The surface statement 'final if heavy, else penult' is my reading of the metrical description plus the transcribed examples; the source itself states the rule only in foot terms.
5177.srule: Stated only for morphology: the transitivity-altering verb prefixes pa 'causative', va (T) ~ wa (O) 'reciprocal', par 'reciprocal' and ma 'detransitivizing' 'seem to be inherently stressed, since they always receives secondary stress, regardless of the canonical shape of the verb root' (p. 7). Rhythmic secondary stresses on non-final feet are implied by the right-to-left bimoraic trochaic footing (p. 6) but are not stated as such, and no transcribed example (pp. 2-9, words up to five syllables) carries a secondary-stress mark, so their placement is not given.

5190.dq: (4) (individual words) a. ngaa ro'o mohii pe'esa- tee te'e ... b. nga ro mohi pesa te te ... This affects the placement of the stress, which is usually penultimate. ... There are three intonational levels in 5a, but only two in 5b.
5190.dloc: p. 714, section 'Tukang Besi', left column: the paragraph 'Phonologically, pidgin Tukang Besi differs from its parent...', example (4) and the stress sentence after it; phrase-intonation remark on ex. (5) at the top of the right column
5190.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable ('usually penultimate'), counted on the surface syllable string: where a speaker contracts V1ʔV1 / V1V1 to V1 (ngaa > nga, ro'o > ro, mohii > mohi, pe'esa > pesa) the syllable count drops and the penult moves accordingly; high vowels in pre-stressed syllables tend to desyllabify (glide), which also changes the count. Same rule as the parent language ('In both languages').
5190.srule: Not mentioned in Donohue 1996:713-716 (section 'Tukang Besi', p. 714; the chapter's only prosodic statements are 'stress... usually penultimate', pre-stress high-vowel desyllabification, and a phrase-intonation remark on ex. (5))
5190.quote: Phonologically, pidgin Tukang Besi differs from its parent in that the imploded stops /ɓ/ and /ɗ/ become /b/ and /d/, and the bilabial fricative that in standard Tukang Besi varies between [β], [ɸ] and [ʋ] becomes [w] in the pidgin. For some speakers V1ʔV1 and V1V1 sequences reduce to V1: (4) (individual words) a. ngaa ro'o mohii pe'esa- tee te'e name leaf left self tea water b. nga ro mohi pesa te te This affects the placement of the stress, which is usually penultimate. In both languages, high vowels tend to desyllabify in pre-stressed syllables, but this is more noticeable in the pidgin.
